wildland fire behavior types
a: Wildland fire behavior encompasses how fires ignite, spread, and intensify in natural fuel beds. Surface fires burn along the ground through grass, duff, brush, and downed timber, typically moving at lower intensities. Crown fires (or canopy fires) burn through the treetops and are the most dangerous and difficult to control, often spreading rapidly via ember transport and radiant heat. Spotting occurs when firebrands (burning twigs, bark, or pine cones) are lofted ahead of the main fire front by convection columns, starting new fires downwind—this can jump firelines and overwhelm containment efforts. Fire whirls are rotating columns of hot air and flame that form in turbulent fire conditions, ranging from small dust-devil-sized vortices to large tornado-strength phenomena capable of uprooting trees and throwing heavy equipment. A blowup is a sudden, dramatic increase in fire intensity caused by changing weather conditions (dry fronts, passing cold fronts, afternoon wind shifts) or topographic effects (chimney effects in canyons, slope alignment with wind), often catching firefighters off guard.

a: The United States wildland firefighting effort is a multi-agency coordination primarily under the National Wildfire Coordinating Group (NWCG). The US Forest Service (USFS), part of the Department of Agriculture, manages fire on 193 million acres of national forests and grasslands and operates the largest wildland firefighting workforce. CAL FIRE (California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection) is the state-level agency responsible for wildfire protection on 31 million acres of California's state and private wildlands, operating the nation's largest state fire department with over 8,000 employees. The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) and National Park Service (NPS) protect their respective federal lands, while the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) manages fire programs on tribal lands. State-level Departments of Natural Resources (DNRs) in states like Washington, Oregon, Minnesota, and Florida coordinate wildfire response on state and private forestlands, often through mutual aid compacts like the Northwest and Great Lakes Forest Fire Compacts.

a: Hand crews are the backbone of wildland firefighting, traveling on foot to construct firelines (mineral soil breaks) using hand tools. Hotshot crews are elite 20-person interagency hand crews (IHCs) that undergo rigorous physical fitness standards and specialized training, serving as rapid-response resources for the most challenging portions of large wildfires. Helitack crews are transported by helicopter to remote fire locations for initial attack, often rappelling from the helicopter to access rugged terrain where landing is impossible, and they also support longline operations and aerial ignition. Smokejumpers are highly specialized firefighters who parachute from fixed-wing aircraft into remote wilderness areas, carrying all necessary supplies for initial attack—they are based at jump bases in key locations like Missoula (Montana), McCall (Idaho), and Redding (California). All hand crew members are certified at minimum as Firefighter Type 2 (FFT2) and progress through qualification levels including squad boss, crew boss, and division supervisor.

wildland firefighting hand tools and equipment
a: Wildland firefighting hand tools are specialized for constructing firelines. The Pulaski, invented by Ed Pulaski after the 1910 fires, combines a grubbing edge (mattock) for cutting roots and mineral soil with an axe blade for chopping limbs—it is the quintessential wildland fire tool. The McLeod is a rake-and-hoe combination used for scraping flammable material from the fireline down to mineral soil. Standard tools also include the shovel (for throwing dirt, cutting small roots, and fireline construction), chainsaws (for felling burning snags and clearing heavy timber), and the drip torch (a canister with a fuel mixture of diesel and gasoline for lighting controlled burns and firing operations). The fire shelter is a mandatory last-resort safety device made of aluminum foil and woven silica cloth that reflects radiant heat and traps breathable air; all wildland firefighters carry one on their person. Portable pumps (Mark 3, Mark 5, and modern high-pressure units like the Honda WX15) are used to relay water from natural sources through hose lays to the fireline, often through thousands of feet of 1-inch lay-flat hose.

a: Wildland fire engines are classified by tank capacity, pump capability, and crew size. Type 3 engines (typically 4x4, 500+ gallon tank, 150+ GPM pump) are designed for off-road travel and direct attack on wildland fires. Type 4 engines (750+ gallons, 50+ GPM) are primarily used for water supply. Type 5 and Type 6 engines are smaller 4x4 units (150-400 gallons) with high-pressure pumps, designed for quick initial attack on steep, narrow roads—Type 6 is the most common initial attack engine on USFS and BLM lands. Air tankers are fixed-wing aircraft that drop fire retardant (a phosphate-based slurry that coats vegetation and slows combustion), ranging from single-engine Air Tractor 802s (800 gallons) to large DC-10 and 747 Very Large Air Tankers (up to 19,600 gallons). Water scoopers like the CL-415 SuperScooper collect water by skimming across lakes, enabling rapid turnaround without returning to an air base. Firefighting helicopters include Type 1 heavy-lift ships (Sikorsky S-64 Skycrane, CH-47 Chinook) that transport water via Bambi Buckets or internal tanks, Type 2 medium helicopters (Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk, Bell 214), and Type 3 light helicopters (Bell 206, AStar) used for reconnaissance and crew transport. Lead planes are small, fast aircraft that coordinate air tanker drops, marking target areas with smoke and ensuring safe separation between aircraft.

q: What are wildland fire suppression strategies?
What is direct attack in wildland firefighting?
What is indirect attack?
What is a burnout operation?
What is a backfire?
What is a firing operation?
What is a fireline?
What is a containment line?
direct attack indirect attack burnout backfire
firing operation fireline containment line
a: Wildland fire suppression strategies fall into two main categories. Direct attack involves firefighters working directly at the fire's edge, applying water, retardant, or hand-constructed fireline right at the flame front—this is the preferred method for low-to-moderate intensity fires in accessible terrain. Indirect attack establishes firelines at a distance from the active fire, using natural barriers (rivers, rock slides, ridges) or constructed firebreaks to stop the fire's spread, typically used for fast-moving, high-intensity fires where direct attack is unsafe. Burnout (or firing out) is a tactic where firefighters deliberately ignite unburned fuel between a control line and the main fire, consuming the intervening vegetation to widen the firebreak. Backfire is a larger-scale controlled ignition set ahead of the main fire front, intended to create such a large burned area that the advancing fire runs out of fuel—this high-risk tactic requires precise timing, favorable winds, and extensive planning under the Incident Command System.

q: What is the Incident Command System for wildland fires?
What is ICS in wildland firefighting?

Incident Command System ICS NIMS Incident Commander Division Strike Team
a: The Incident Command System (ICS) is a standardized, all-hazards management approach used for wildland fires in the United States under the National Incident Management System (NIMS). ICS establishes a clear chain of command with the Incident Commander (IC) at the top, supported by four General Staff sections: Operations (tactical firefighting), Planning (resource tracking and future projections), Logistics (supplies, food, shelter, medical), and Finance (cost tracking and procurement). Large wildland fires are organized geographically into Divisions (land-based) and Groups (functional, like air operations), further subdivided into Branches, with resources organized as Strike Teams (same type, e.g., five engines) or Task Forces (mixed resources, e.g., two engines, a water tender, and a hand crew). This modular system allows ICS to scale from a single-engine initial attack to thousands of personnel on a complex incident like the Thomas Fire or August Complex.

a: Wildland fire season has lengthened dramatically due to climate change—historically concentrated in late summer and fall (June-October in the western US), fire season now overlaps with spring and extends well into winter in many regions, with some areas experiencing year-round fire risk. Notable wildfires include the Yellowstone Fires of 1988 (which burned 1.4 million acres in and around Yellowstone National Park, transforming fire management policy to recognize fire's natural ecological role). California has experienced the deadliest and most destructive wildfires in US history: the Camp Fire (2018) destroyed the town of Paradise, killed 85 people, and burned over 18,000 structures; the August Complex (2020) burned over 1 million acres across seven counties; and the Thomas Fire (2017) burned 281,000 acres in Ventura and Santa Barbara counties. Australia's Black Saturday bushfires (2009) killed 173 people and burned over 2,000 homes in Victoria, while the 2019-2020 Australian bushfire season (the Black Summer) burned an estimated 46 million acres, killed 34 people, and devastated koala populations and vast forest ecosystems. Historically, the Peshtigo Fire (1871) in Wisconsin killed 1,500-2,500 people—the deadliest wildfire in American history—and the Great Fire of 1910 (the Big Burn) burned 3 million acres across Idaho and Montana, leading to the establishment of modern wildland firefighting policies.

a: LCES is the foundational wildland firefighter safety system, developed after the 1994 South Canyon Fire (Storm King Mountain) tragedy that killed 14 firefighters. Lookouts are personnel positioned to monitor fire behavior changes and warn crews of emerging threats; Communications ensures everyone shares a common radio frequency, uses clear terminology, and continuously updates conditions; Escape Routes are pre-identified paths from the fireline to Safety Zones, cleared of obstacles and marked with flagging; Safety Zones are areas large enough to shelter personnel without fire shelters (usually at least four times the flame height in diameter). These four elements must be continuously re-evaluated as conditions change. Fire weather plays a critical role in firefighter safety: Red Flag Warnings are issued by the National Weather Service when conditions (low humidity, high winds, dry fuels) create extreme fire danger; Santa Ana winds in Southern California and Diablo winds in Northern California are hot, dry downslope winds that can drive explosive fire growth; and the National Fire Danger Rating System (NFDRS) provides daily indices based on weather, fuel moisture, and topography to guide preparedness levels.
